description: Ishmael signs on to the Pequod to hunt Moby Dick. Melville mixes sea adventure, the science of whales, and a meditation on obsession.

hero.hook: Call me Ishmael: three words that open one of the cathedrals of American literature.

blocks.text: Published in **1851**, **Moby-Dick** is far more than a sea adventure. Its full original title is *Moby-Dick; or, The Whale*. **Herman Melville**, who was born in **1819** and died in **1891**, mixes epic, a treatise on whales, and metaphysical questions. Misunderstood when it came out, this monument of [[American literature]] has become a founding myth.

The novel explores the huge struggle between man, nature, and the divine, through the hunt for a legendary white whale. Its opening line, “Call me Ishmael,” is one of the most famous in all of literature.

**Herman Melville** sailed on whaleships in the Pacific in the **1840s**. He even lived among the tribes of the [[Marquesas]], an archipelago in French Polynesia. Drawing on that experience, he wrote his great book between **1850** and **1851**, in a house he shared with **Nathaniel Hawthorne**.

blocks.caption: Herman Melville, forgotten in his lifetime, rediscovered in the 20th century

blocks.text: When he died in **1891**, Melville was so completely forgotten that the New York Times ran an obituary for “Henry Melville.”

The novel was a complete commercial failure. Melville died convinced that his name would disappear. Only in the 20th century did he enter the [[literary canon]], the set of works held to be fundamental and worth teaching.

sections.title: Melville and the failure of a total book

blocks.text: “Call me Ishmael”: the narrator signs on to the **Pequod** at [[New Bedford]]. In the 19th century that town was the whaling capital of the world. The ship is American society in miniature, with sailors from everywhere. [[Queequeg]], a tattooed Polynesian harpooner, is the son of an island chief.

blocks.caption: Hunting the [[sperm whale]]: Melville gives whole chapters to [[cetology]]

blocks.text: The mates [[Starbuck]], a level-headed Quaker, [[Stubb]], calm and cheerful, and [[Flask]], all impulse, stand for different faces of reason. Captain **Ahab** imposes iron discipline in the service of a secret obsession: hunting down the whale that tore off his leg.

sections.title: The Pequod, a social and industrial world in miniature

blocks.text: **Moby Dick** is a white [[sperm whale]], an unbeatable [[Leviathan]]. That biblical sea monster carries colossal power. For **Ahab**, it is not an animal but the mask of cosmic [[Malignity]], a deliberate wickedness he reads into the whole universe. Having lost his leg, he devotes his life to hunting Evil itself.

blocks.caption: The Pequod facing the ocean: a trading voyage turned theological quest

blocks.text: Melville uses [[spermaceti]], the waxy substance lodged in the sperm whale's head, to underline how indifferent nature is. Whiteness stands for a terrifying emptiness, a universe that gives no answer. Every character reads his own demons into the whale.

sections.title: The white whale as a mirror of the absolute

blocks.text: In the last assault, Moby Dick smashes the Pequod to pieces. Ahab dies strangled by his own harpoon line. Ishmael alone survives, afloat on Queequeg's coffin, picked up by the whaleship **Rachel**. The rest of the crew goes down into the ocean.

Ishmael's survival is what makes the book possible. The survivor bears witness to human madness and to the untamable power of nature. If a man cannot defeat the unknown, he can at least tell the story of it. Melville mixes sea adventure, a whale encyclopedia, and a meditation on destructive obsession. Whole chapters set out [[cetology]], the study of cetaceans, with almost scientific precision, before the book tips into tragedy.
**Moby-Dick** turns the hunt for a sperm whale into a philosophical odyssey about Ahab's obsession and the indifference of a universe that Ishmael alone lives to describe.

sections.title: The final wreck, and survival through storytelling
